title: How employment is changing at Anthropic
article_text:
Nathan Wilmers, Regina Catipon, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.
Key findings
- Anthropic has been hiring for a smaller share of junior technical positions. This occurred as hours worked by AI agents relative to employees rapidly expanded. By August interactive AI agent hours outnumbered employees’ six to one.
- As AI agents diffused through the company, Anthropic began producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts. Following the same employee over time, output rose as they adopted new AI tools.
- This acceleration makes human attention the bottleneck for agent output. Even among non-technical employees, reading all the output of their Claude agents would take half their work week. In response, employees turn to “meta-work,” of building visibility tools and monitoring agent pipelines.
- Changes in work organization are reflected in shifting priorities among hiring managers, who increasingly emphasize autonomy and judgment, relative to technical domain expertise and implementation.
Introduction
What transformations of work and employment can we expect under increasingly powerful AI? Anthropic is worth studying because it has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI. Agents flit through Slack chats and schedule meetings. They autonomously fix bugs and collectively tackle huge engineering projects. Agent hours worked outnumber human hours 6 to 1. Changes happening at Anthropic now give advanced signals about a possible future of work and employment.
This report draws on comprehensive internal Anthropic data covering employment, AI use, output metrics, employee surveys, internal communication patterns, employee calendar data, and hiring decision records. It contextualizes these quantitative data with 17 employee interviews.
We find that even as the company grows, relative hiring in junior technical positions has slowed. Productivity for both engineers and non-technical employees has leapt up and did so sharply when they adopted coding agents. Hiring managers increasingly emphasize applicants’ autonomy and judgment relative to specific technical expertise. A defining feature of working in an AI-heavy organization is constant pressure to streamline oneself out of this bottleneck position when possible. One engineer described work as facing “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention.” Employees at Anthropic remain critical. But the nature of their contributions has changed.
Anthropic has responded to these changes by setting up an early warning system to track jobs at risk of disruption, and as jobs evolve the company has prioritized internal redeployments. These actions, taken at the frontier of both AI development and workplace change, show how specific organizational commitments can shape the impact of AI on employment. But they also raise difficult questions about exactly what those commitments should be.
Labor demand at the frontier
Anthropic has expanded rapidly. But it has hired less per dollar of revenue than an earlier generation of large tech companies. At five years old, Anthropic takes in between 2–4 times as much revenue per employee as Meta and Google as they crested in their own rapid growth.1
What jobs are missing? Within Anthropic, discussion of a decline in demand for junior technical employees emerged in core technical functions in January 2026. The teams that relied most heavily on Claude in their own work found that writing code and finding bugs could increasingly be offloaded to Claude. Newly capable models accelerated this perception: “the thing that raised eyebrows was the uplift for performance engineers in particular and it basically overnight changed what we were looking for.”
By April, engineering and research teams had deemphasized hiring for lower band technical positions. When surveyed in the same month, a majority of managers described hiring for a different set of skills due to AI. Around a third of ML and a fifth of SWE managers reported hiring less due to AI.
The shift in employment shares is striking. Figure 1 shows that the share of junior-level employees in technical departments at Anthropic slipped from 21% to 14% since early 2025. The proportion of junior technical hires fell even faster, from 27% to 9%. Postings for juniors have fallen particularly sharply since December 2025.
At the same time, the overall employment share of technical departments within Anthropic has fallen, from 61% to 56% in the last year. As the company expands, technical hiring has continued growing in absolute terms, but intensive hiring in sales, finance, and recruiting has outpaced it. Part of this shift is the natural expansion of business functions as the company scales. Part could reflect coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves. For example, a sales representative designed a custom dashboard and pipeline tailored to their work: “a build like this was out of my wheelhouse, especially with the UI, connecting all the tools, the MCPs. But I built this probably in three to four hours, just iterating on it.” Coding-focused AI agent sessions for non-technical employees (identified as those with no code commits at baseline, excluding new hires) leapt from 2 per month in August 2025 to 90 in May 2026.
Yet this shift in hiring composition is not only a story about automated coding allowing it to diffuse to other domain experts. Within technical departments, the share of employees not actively coding (defined as those making no code commits in the prior 30 days) fell by almost half over the year through April 2026. Part of this is due to a thinning share of non-engineers: the ratio of engineers to product managers, for example, sits at around 17 to 1 and has increased since 2025. The number of commits from managers has also doubled. The supervising and coordinating roles within technical teams increasingly involve building and shipping code.
One area in which non-technical hiring has not accelerated is in the administrative functions that typically scale with a company’s size. A combination of agent assistants, automated review and ticket service outsourcing has left Anthropic clerical-light even as it has grown rapidly. A financial manager built a purchase request review agent and explained to colleagues “it's just trying to find the things that take a lot of hours so they can focus on the other stuff.”
Even clerical work tightly connected to in-person interaction has grown slowly. An executive assistant, who built a personal assistant agent for scheduling and email triage, explained: “I think we've already moved past the point of Claude augmenting away the really entry-level admin type role,” and instead focused their work on higher-order “chief of staff” tasks.
These changes have already involved reallocation: employees working at the company for at least a year were 50% more likely to move across departments each month in 2026 than they were in 2025. Whole teams have also been reallocated as they handed off their work to agents. Consider one product design team, which wrote content like the greetings on Claude.ai: “Hello night owl;” “Coffee and Claude time?” In spring 2026, the team developed a context graph that effectively guided agents to write compelling product content. This “scaled the team out,” its manager explained, but also raised the question of what was left for human writers. The team then rotated into agent prompting and began writing model evals and prompts for Claude. “Writers who used language to drive human behavior are now using it to drive Claude behavior.”
Is AI driving productivity increases at Anthropic?
Are these shifts attributable to AI? At Anthropic, humans are a thin layer atop a growing contingent of AI agents. Based on agent session telemetry, in March 2026, the sum of autonomous and interactive agent work hours leapt past human work hours for the first time. Part of this is fleets of agents conducting industrial-scale software engineering, filling in myriad routine tests and checks, conducting maintenance on a growing mass of infrastructure code, and driving concerted campaigns to translate massive codebases. But even narrowing in on the agents deployed by individual employees, as in Figure 2, by August the agents worked 6 times as many hours as their human handlers.
Anthropic is a software producer, and the vast bulk of tokens flowing through these agents is spent producing software code. Dashboards monitor fleets of agents operating across the company. But personal assistant agents also monitor employee calendars and messages, scheduling, sending to-do lists accumulated from incoming messages, and automatically briefing employees on the people and purpose of their upcoming meetings. Tokens touch a growing range of everyday work tasks.
What do all of these tokens amount to? Figure 3 plots output over time for a range of job functions with measurable output. Consistent with prior reports surveying Anthropic engineers and describing automation of model training and research, code commits per engineer have risen the fastest, coming in at 5x their velocity as six months ago. Data scientists are also querying the growing mass of Anthropic data more, asking Claude agents to get real-time metrics to dashboards and decisionmakers. But Figure 3 shows that even non-technical employees saw output rise as coding agents diffused: lawyers processed more contracts; accounts payable ushered through invoices; salespeople closed more deals.
But is all of this due to Claude usage? During this same period, the company saw explosive business growth. It is easier to close deals when you sell a strong model. To assess the independent effect of AI, we compare the output of employees who adopt agentic coding tools to those who have not yet adopted the tools. This lets us compare employees working in the same month at the company, and therefore exposed to a similar business context, but approaching it with different tools. Note, however, that tool adoption is not random: if employees on the cusp of driving some big new project decide to tool up for it, for example, this would bias our estimates.
We follow 192 engineers over time as they adopt coding agents, compared to 74 engineers who do not adopt agents during the period studied. Figure 4 shows that in the months following adoption, the amount of code that engineers add rises sharply. More code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact. To test for AI code slop, we study code commits made at Anthropic. We compare code committed by the same employee, in the same month, in the same coding directory, but written by coding agents rather than written directly by the human employee. There are many dimensions of code quality, and AI errors may be harder to identify than human ones. But we find no difference in rates of lines of code subsequently removed or reverted.
Figure 4 also looks at what happens after an engineer adopts their first fully autonomous agent. Those who adopt were already on a steeply upward trajectory compared to non-adopters. This suggests that employees shifting toward fully autonomous agents were already ramping up their output.
Do these patterns go beyond coding, into a broader transformation of knowledge work? Anthropic sales representatives steadily adopted AI agents starting last September. Figure 4 shows that after sales representatives adopt agents, they close deals with more clients. Part of this pattern could be driven by representatives with more sales opportunities selecting into automation. But it could also reflect automation of logging and routine communication. One account executive explained that Claude automations handled email drafting and customer management software integrations, replacing around 20% of their prior work tasks. Another noted that similar automations freed them up to focus on face-to-face time, letting them talk to 30% more of their customers than was previously possible: “anytime you do anything a second time, you're kind of like, okay, how can I use Claude to make it so that I don't have to do it a third time?”
Beyond sales, an Anthropic lawyer built a series of Claude automations to scan risks and opportunities, triage legal questions and take first passes through public-facing copy for legal review. A recruiter used Claude to help with candidate sourcing, tracking applications and an analysis that would have taken “maybe a couple of weeks,” freeing him to redesign outdated interview questions and meet with more applicants.
All of this suggests that as AI capabilities improve, it impacts a wide range of jobs across Anthropic. Descriptively, we see junior employment slowing in jobs that use Claude for the most complex tasks (Figure 5).
Bottlenecks and process: new and old tasks in an AI-intensive workplace
Heavy AI adoption reshapes more than employment and productivity. It also drives continual changes in work processes, generating new tasks and shifting employees’ perceptions of their workplace. One employee described this as the “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything” and another that “things we expect in a week are things that would take three months elsewhere.” An internal employee survey asked whether work processes at Anthropic made respondents as productive as possible: 44% of employees agreed in late 2024; 58% by November 2025 (in April 2026, 75% answered yes, but the question weakened by dropping “as possible”). As of August, employees at Anthropic expected that AI will be able to do 75% of their work by 2030, compared to 28% for other Americans.
These ratcheting productivity expectations are dramatized by the cadence of internal model releases. As soon as a new model is available, Anthropic employees start tackling harder problems in interactive coding agent sessions. We measure this with an automated Claude grader rating deidentified sessions’ task demands based on depth, scope and number of systems implicated. The share of tasks above the 90th percentile of difficulty for the old model rises sharply by around 30% (from 10% to 13% of all tasks) and stays elevated in the weeks following model releases. The easy end of tasks given to agents changes little.
Spiraling agent productivity translates into output pitched across humans’ screens and attention. One engineer compared this to babysitting:
They're like, I need my juice box opened and it's an emergency that my juice box is opened. And that is voiced with the same level of concern as the one who has sliced their finger and is bleeding. [...] When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.
In the April 2026 survey, an open-ended question about how AI has impacted day-to-day work, 27% described productivity gains from Claude tools and 20% described their role shifting from actually doing work to managing Claudes.
Amid this model-driven acceleration, human attention is a constant bottleneck. In interactive, multi-turn sessions, the vast majority of agents’ session time is not spent working at all, but spent waiting. We track idle time by subtracting each agent’s active working time from each interactive session’s total wall-clock time. Claude sessions amount to around 80% idly waiting for human input. As one engineer put it, people are “bottlenecking the agents.”
How much time exactly would be needed to read all of Claude’s output from interactive sessions? For each interactive session, we convert each session’s agent output token to word count, assuming average human reading speed. Figure 6 shows that technical functions have seen the volume of coding agent output leap up over the last six months. But even for non-technical groups, interactive Claude sessions are outputting enough content to take up over half of the work week. The deluge of Claude text needs organizing.
One solution to this deluge is rising automation. But this requires work of a different kind. Written standing instructions for agents grew from a few hundred in July 2025 to 8,500 a year later. One engineer set up an agent chief of staff to triage agent requests. Another wrote a performance review for their Claude team: “Hey, let’s talk about what is and is not working about our communication style.” Recruiters built integrated dashboards with agents surfacing problems and initiating actions. A lawyer shifted their attention from reviewing legal questions to doing “SEO for legal advice, you need to write frameworks that [clients’] agents discover.”
Figure 7 shows that this kind of meta-work leapt from 10% of the average employee’s interactive Claude sessions in fall 2025 to 22% in spring 2026. Much of this rise was due specifically to agent management: writing specs for multi-agent runs, looping one agent to review another’s output, and monitoring pipelines. Across functions, human involvement increasingly abstracted from a particular piece of code or writing to the tooling necessary to get agents to do their tasks effectively.
Despite increases in agent reliability and these significant investments in tooling to supervise them, human trust and accountability remains critical. One employee explained that, increasingly, chasing down bugs “uncovers these organizational or systemic or tech debt things that actually require some amount of human convening and decision-making and governance to solve.” In interview after interview, employees described face-to-face coordination as indispensable. Based on calendar data, the median employee spends 20% more time in meetings than a year ago. Part of this reflects the growth of the company, and a shift toward meeting-intensive non-technical roles. But even among employees in technical individual contributor roles, meeting time is up 16% over the past year. Big-picture strategic questions touch a broad range of leveraged positions, and typically require debate and engagement with others. A break from managing the agents typically looks like jumping into a meeting.
Broadly, both technical and non-technical roles have seen implementation parts of their job automated (writing code, identifying bugs, logging progress, drafting emails). Engineers described becoming leaders and managers of agents; non-technical employees described doing more and more of the strategic parts of their job: “that 20% that was strategic becomes 90% of the job.” But for many non-technical roles, core implementation work is also interpersonal: a sales call, an interview, cross-functional alignment on a complex problem. All of this remains human.
Consider too the Slack channels that provide both the front page and backchannels of Anthropic communication. Agents diffused through Slack and eventually appeared in nearly half of active, public channels. Figure 8 zooms in on the communication network of a single large department, drawing on all public Slack channels that department members interacted through. It links both human and agent participants by whether they participated in a Slack thread. The figure shows the remarkable rise of agents, as orange dots blossom and dominate the network.
Agents appear disproportionately in dedicated channels for Claude-human interactions, rather than messaging a lot in incumbent human channels. The underlying structure and density of human communication changes little. Agents did not replace human interaction, but rather added to it: human threads in this department sustained the same number of human responses, while additionally layering on agent responses. Agents become teams for a single employee, rather than nodes with high connectivity to many employees at once.
As humans work amid a growing fleet of AI agents, they face pressure to shift human work into agent-visible channels. If a decision is made in an in-person meeting, and no notes or report-out appears, agents are missing crucial context for updating their goals and assumptions. An employee explained how having their name on a months-old document about Claude swag meant agents kept bringing requests for t-shirts and mugs, long after their responsibilities had changed. Private work, in unlogged meetings and direct messages, is invisible, confusing and discouraged in an AI-heavy workplace. One researcher described this default toward openness as critical to Anthropic’s thoroughgoing integration of AI: “most organizations do not run that way and I think that's a big shift because leaders have to defend feedback out in the open.” The need to feed AI context requires observability of human work and decisions.
Who will thrive in a workplace like this? Shifts in the content of work at Anthropic also show up as changes in the skills that hiring managers prioritize in hiring decisions. We used an automated coder to process hiring manager interview score cards for thousands of employees hired at Anthropic since 2024. These comments are qualitative reactions by interviewers assessing candidates’ performance. The clearest change is increased emphasis on whether candidates have demonstrated creative use of AI tools. In 2024, hiring managers noted candidates' track record on AI tooling in around 5% of assessments for technical roles, and 7% for non-technical roles. By 2026, these rates had tripled for technical roles and quadrupled for non-technical roles. Hiring managers increasingly focus on whether candidates effectively use AI.
Deeper changes in assessment are also visible. Among interviews for technical candidates, the single biggest increases were in comments on applicants’ autonomy and judgment. Discussion of domain expertise shrank as a share of overall assessment. As one manager explained, “I expect models to continue to be jagged, so for my team I want them to be fungible across domains.” Similarly, for non-technical candidates, customer and mission orientation increased, while discussion of execution skills fell. Increasingly, hiring managers assess applicants based on their judgment and commitment, rather than the domain-specific skills and execution automated by AI tools.
What employers can do
The deep adoption of AI at Anthropic makes it a useful case. As AI diffuses and improves, the organization of work could shift as it has in prior waves of technological change. The railroads gave us the managerial corporation, steam power allowed factories, and personal computers delivered the startup. What new organizations will tool-using, reasoning LLMs require, and what will be our role in them? One possibility is single-person startups, each with a human founder steering swarms of agents to rake in billions in revenue. Another is companies built by AI genius CEOs employing human agents only to wield pipettes and testify before Congress.
Anthropic does not look like either of these. It has tripled in size in the last year. It is no longer a small startup. It has also not ceded executive control to its models. Written Slack debates and in-person meetings steer everything from company strategy to team decisions, with little input from AI agents. Keeping human work visible across the company ensures autonomous agents reason from fresh context. Individual contributors orchestrating teams of agents look more like managers in terms of the knowledge they need and the interdependencies in their work. Working and deciding in the open is critical at an AI-intensive organization.
As employees increasingly see their work as managing teams of Claudes, they spend more time building the tools needed to do this effectively in their own distinctive domains. This experimentation means that employees are continually automating their own tasks away. In some roles, they are increasingly removed from the object-level work that originally built their skills. As agents sprint through workflows, human attention and judgment are a bottleneck that the system strains against. From sales to legal, human employees are expected to do more and different tasks. Roles broaden to include building products, managing agents and tackling the strategic and interpersonal work that remain beyond the scope of the best LLMs.
These changes in the organization and content of work have appeared alongside declining shares of junior technical roles in headcount, hiring, and posting. Hiring managers increasingly focus on applicants’ autonomy and judgment, rather than execution and narrow expertise. Overall, Anthropic’s revenue growth relative to its employment growth has sped past even the rapid early productivity growth of a prior generation of technology companies.
Reading these patterns forward and out across the economy suggests that AI diffusion could risk worker displacement. Prior work also finds that AI-native startups and AI-adopters are flatter and employ fewer entry-level employees. What can we learn from Anthropic about how to manage AI upheavals in a way that serves the humans working around them?
Here we want to proceed carefully. There are many parts of Anthropic’s employment practices that cannot be replicated across the economy.
But three features stand out. First, widespread stock ownership gives employees a strong interest in the company’s success. Of course, this is an easy posture for a company that has seen substantial increases in valuation. For many firms, shared ownership may be insufficient or otherwise undesirable. But it is difficult to imagine a version of pro-worker AI adoption in which workers do not hold a financial stake in successful rollout. If individual contributors are expected to “manage agents,” “make VP-level decisions” and be “their own business line,” as interviewees put it, then aligning their interests with the organization is crucial. The post-World War II union-management settlement forged in the 1950s rested on exactly this kind of bargain: labor unions like the United Auto Workers and the United Steel Workers allowed management prerogative over work reorganization (and even intensification) in return for pay increases tied to productivity increases and to a rich array of benefits. Whatever the new deal between AI-affected employees and their employers, a mechanism to share benefits of adoption is essential. At Anthropic, workers codify their expertise for the machine, see their work routines constantly roiled and disrupted, and have seen a large part of their job become speedreading the output of their AI collaborators. They do not do this for free.
Second, Anthropic is standing up an ongoing early warning system to monitor jobs facing AI-driven transformation. A series of role-level metrics for demand and productivity are read against AI capabilities and use. These aggregate metrics help flag where work is shifting. An early warning system allows the company to start reallocating affected employees to jobs with a skills fit that may be less immediately at risk. As companies across the economy reorient to an accelerated pace of work reorganization, effective systems for guiding internal employee reallocation will become increasingly valuable. Turning to the external labor market to meet every new task demanded by AI advances will be a stronger bottleneck the faster AI advances. In this report, we found increased mobility between departments, changing work content, and employees shifting to new tasks as old ones were automated. Building systems to flexibly reallocate workers internally will be critical for AI-intensive organizations.
This commitment to internal worker reallocation raises important tradeoffs. A well-functioning labor market should shift workers into their most productive positions, whether that is at their current employer or another one. Commitments to reallocate incumbent workers could make employers hesitant to take a risk on hiring new employees. In normal economic conditions, particularly intensely competitive ones, such commitments could be costly.
But prioritizing reallocation forces AI-adopting companies to consider ways that AI can create new tasks for new products and new markets, rather than funneling AI applications into replacing human workers to save on labor costs. This could help employers resist the temptation of ‘so-so’ or ‘inefficient’ automation in which AI or other technologies just barely outcompete human workers: employers replace human workers, imposing substantial social costs in lost income for displaced workers, while delivering minimal productivity benefits.
From what we see in Anthropic, both novel and persistently human tasks remain alongside intensive AI use. Uncertainty about the future set of these tasks should recommend preserving a flexible workforce. As one Anthropic executive noted, “a workforce that is anxiously worried is not a workforce doing its best work.”
None of these actions will prevent powerful AI from disrupting jobs. And indeed none directly address the slowdown in junior hires documented in this report. Employment protections for incumbents will not benefit those not hired to begin with. Private action on the part of employers must come alongside farsighted government policy around retraining and income support. Such policy should be guided by a clear picture of the scale of workplace transformation that AI can bring.

title: Unleashing the productivity revolution with AI agents that work across your entire stack | IBM
article_text:
Emerging AI agents represent a fundamental tipping point in the AI revolution, shifting from AI that can chat with you, to AI that can do work for you—with unprecedented autonomy.
For decades, interacting with powerful enterprise systems required specialized knowledge to navigate a vast network of complex interfaces. AI agents will lower the barrier to accessing AI's power. By enabling interaction through conversational interfaces, users can simply state their goals—while networks of agents take on the necessary actions across backend systems. This democratization means every person, regardless of their technical expertise, can leverage AI to automate complex tasks, gain insights and drive productivity across functions like HR, finance, IT and customer service.
We believe this new operating model will be the catalyst that ignites the massive economic potential anticipated for generative AI—which has been estimated to generate up to USD 4.4 trillion economic value annually across industries, according to McKinsey.
But to make it a reality, agents must be able to work seamlessly across the vast web of applications, data and systems that underpin today's complex enterprise technology stacks. Which means that orchestration, integration and automation are the secret weapons that will move agents from novelty into operation.
That’s why IBM isn’t just making agents—we're re-imagining the underlying technology stack that will power the agent era.
IBM’s strategy is all about helping clients put agents to work across all their technologies, on any infrastructure, powered by all their data. Our portfolio enables businesses to orchestrate agents from any vendor and platforms like Salesforce Agentforce, while also leveraging the power of their existing IT estate–including technologies from Adobe, Microsoft, Oracle, ServiceNow, Workday and more. And to do it quickly, with pre-built agents, tools and integrations.
Today, we’re unveiling the most comprehensive set of agent capabilities in the industry to help companies build, run and manage agents—delivered via IBM watsonx Orchestrate.
Core to this strategy is IBM watsonx Orchestrate, our unified solution to orchestrate work across your entire enterprise landscape. It functions as a multi-agent supervisor, router, and planner, enabling agents–whether from IBM, third-party platforms or open source–to collaborate effectively with each other and with your existing assets (traditional automations, AI assistants, APIs, data stores, and applications). It’s pre-integrated with 80+ leading enterprise applications, making it the ideal gateway for infusing agents across the full enterprise stack—no vendor lock-in.

title: 2026 Work Trend Index report: Agents, human agency, and opportunity
article_text:
As AI and agents take on execution,
our own agency expands.
The question is whether
organizations are built to capture it.
The opportunity for human potential at work has never been greater. People are using AI and agents to expand what they can do and who gets to do it, and new research shows thatâs only accelerating. Call it the new agency equation: as agents take on more of the execution, humans increasingly have more agencyâmore room to direct the work, make the calls, and own the outcomes. For every firm, the imperative now is to turn that agency into unprecedented value.
We analyzed trillions of anonymized Microsoft 365 productivity signals and surveyed 20,000 workers using AI1 across 10 countries. We also spoke with leading experts in AI, work, and organizational psychology to help us unpack the insights from the data and understand where all this is going. The anxiety around AIÂ at work is realâfrom fears of job loss to the pressureÂ to keep up with rapidly evolving technology. But our research shows something else: that a growing share of workers are using AI in advanced, resourceful ways. The problem? Most organizations arenât keeping up.
In many cases, people are ready. The systems around them are not.
The constraintÂ for most firmsÂ isÂ theÂ gap between whatÂ theirÂ employees can now do and what their organizations are built toÂ support.Â Our data shows that organizational factorsâculture, manager support, talent practicesâaccount for twice the reported AI impact2 of individual effort alone.
Bridging that gap meansÂ redesigningÂ the operating model across employees, leaders, and the organization.Â The ones already doing itâFrontier Firmsâare pulling ahead fast. EmployeesÂ are using AI to lift theÂ ceiling on what they can do. Leaders are rearchitecting work itself, deciding what humans and AI do. And organizations are turning into Learning Systemsâbecause the companies that learn fastest from their own work will be the ones that win.
HereâsÂ whatÂ Frontier Firms doÂ differentlyâand how we can all take control of what comes next.
Employees
AI is expanding what we can doâand putting a premium on judgment, clarity of intent, and the design of work itself.
AÂ privacy-preservingÂ analysisÂ ofÂ more thanÂ 100,000 chats in Microsoft 365 Copilot shows that 49% of all conversations support cognitive workâhelping workers analyze information, solve problems, evaluate, and think creatively. The remainder splits among working with people (19%), finding information (15%), and producing work (17%).3
From expertise to agency
NearlyÂ half of Microsoft 365 Copilot chat use supports analysis, decisions, and problem-solvingâthe kind of high-value work that onceÂ requiredÂ deepÂ expertise. The rest helps people work with others (19%), produce outputs (17%), and find information (15%).
Employees at every level now have a partner that helps them analyze, synthesize, and deepen their own expertise, while also building expertise in other areas. AI is not just helping us do things faster. Itâs expanding who can do high-value work.
The data backs this up: 66% of AI users we surveyed4 say AI has allowed them to spend more time on high-value work and 58% say theyâre producing work they couldnât have a year ago.
That rises toÂ 80%Â amongÂ Frontier Professionals,Â the most advanced AI users in ourÂ research.Â Frontier Professionals use agents for multi-step workflows and building multi-agent systems. They routinely rethink workflows and identify where agents can augment or automate. And theyÂ participateÂ inâ¯practices like creating shared AI standards for their team or organization. TheyÂ represent a small but disproportionately valuable group:Â 16%Â of the AI users we surveyed.
Frontier ProfessionalsÂ refuse to outsource their thinkingâthey know long-term success meansÂ continuing to buildÂ human skillsÂ andÂ notÂ letting themÂ atrophy.
But as AI expandsÂ whatÂ peopleÂ can do, it also raises the premium on good judgment. Most AI users we surveyed recognize this.Â Asked which human skills are more important as AI takes on more work, they said two topped the list: quality control of AI output (50%) and critical thinkingâanalyzing information objectively and making a reasoned judgment (46%). And 86% say they treat AI output as a starting point, not a final answer, and that they âstay responsible for the thinking.â They see their role is shifting from generating answers to evaluating, refining, and owningÂ them.
Frontier ProfessionalsÂ are even more aware of the importance of human judgment when working with AI. They rank higher across every measure in the survey related to critical thinking and quality controlâand that shows up in how they work. They are more likely than non-Frontier professionals to say they intentionally do some work without AI to keep their skills sharp (43%Â vs. 30%) and to say they intentionally pause before starting work to decide what should be done by AI versus a human (53%Â vs.Â 33%).Â Frontier ProfessionalsÂ refuse to outsource their thinkingâthey know long-term success meansÂ continuing to buildÂ human skills and not letting them atrophy.
Beyond the prompt
How people work with AI depends on two thingsâhow they engage with the work, and how much they use the agent. Four modes fall out: delegation, collaboration, asking, and exploration.
Illustrative framework developed by the WTI 2026 research team, informed by patterns in Microsoft 365 Copilot usage and survey findings on how Frontier Professionals describe their AI work. This is a conceptual framework, not a data visualization; the placement of each mode is qualitative.
AsÂ AIÂ useÂ matures across all employees, theÂ most effective AI usersÂ wonâtÂ be the ones who do more things faster. TheyâllÂ be the ones who redefine their value around what only humans can do: setting clear intentâdefining the desired outcome and quality barâand designing how the work gets doneÂ across humans and AI. They apply judgment and taste, build trust, and shape systems that produce better outcomes. The question stops being âWhat tasks define my job?â and starts being âWhat outcomes am I now positioned to drive?â
Aneesh Raman
Chief Economic Opportunity Officer
Dr. Laura Hamill
Director of Research, AI@Work Thought Leadership
Microsoft
Conor Grennan
CEO and Founder
AI Mindset
Leaders
MostÂ organizations are not yet built to capture the value of this expanded human agency. The challenge is not isolated to tools or individualsâitâsÂ a breakdown across the system that connects leadership, culture, management practices, and how work is measured.
To understand where this breakdown occurs, we mapped survey respondents across two dimensions: their capability with AI and their organizationâs readiness to absorb it.
In many cases,Â employees are moving faster than the organizations around them.
Individual capabilityÂ reflects how broadly respondents report using AI and how confidently they direct it, judge its output, and learn from it. It alsoÂ includesÂ how actively they experiment and share learnings, and whether they report creating new value with AIâfrom improving work quality and processes to enabling work theyÂ couldnâtÂ do before.
Organizational readiness reflects the environment around them, including: culture and management practices that support AI use, clear rules and guidelines for how people and AI work together, and whether AI use is encouraged and recognized.
The Transformation Paradox
Roughly 1 in 5 workers are in the Frontier zone, where individual capability and organizational readiness reinforce each other. About 1 in 10 are blocked: skilled workers in companies thatÂ havenâtÂ yet caught up. About half of all workers sit in theÂ emergentÂ zone in between.

Both axes are self-reported composite scores normalized 0â1 within each market before pooling. Individual readiness combines items from Q1 (self-efficacy), Q4 (AI usage sophistication), Q6 (proactive AI behaviors), and Q22 (value creation). Organizational readiness combines items from Q11 (governance maturity), Q12 (manager support), Q14 (AI in performance evaluation), and Q19 (organizational AI culture). All values are self-reported survey responses; no telemetry or behavioral observation is used.
The results reveal five groups of AI users.Â AndÂ in many cases,Â employees are moving faster than the organizations around them.
OnlyÂ 19%Â of AI usersÂ areÂ Frontier, the sweet spot where organizational capability and individual readiness are both high and reinforcing each other. At the other end, 16% are stalled, with low capability and limited organizational support. The rest are misaligned:Â 10% fall into blocked agency, where individuals have built strong skills but lack the systems to apply them. 5% sit in unclaimed capacity, where organizations are readyÂ but employees have yet to catch up. The largest share sits in theÂ messy middle, or emergent zone, where both individual practice and organizational conditions are still taking shape.
ThisÂ misalignment is reinforced at the top. Only one in four AI users surveyed (26%) say theirÂ leadershipÂ is clearly and consistently aligned on AI. Leaders surveyedÂ are also more likely than employees to say AI-driven reinvention feels safe and rewarded.5
1 in 4
WhatÂ emergesÂ is aÂ pressure point within the organization where theÂ pull to performÂ collides with theÂ push to transform.Â 65%Â ofÂ AI usersÂ fear falling behind if they donât use AI to adapt quickly, yetÂ 45%Â say it feels safer to focus on current goals than to redesign work with AI. And only 13% of AI users say theyâre rewarded for reinvention of work with AI even if results arenât met.
We call this theÂ Transformation Paradox: Employees are ready to reinvent how they work, but the system around themâmetrics, incentives, and normsâcontinues to reinforce the old way.Â The same forcesÂ accelerating AI adoption are holding it back.
The job ofÂ everyÂ leader right now is to makeÂ changeÂ stick. That means setting strategy at the top and ensuring the metrics, incentives, and expectations reward people for changing the way they work.
Once that strategy is set,Â itâsÂ managers whoÂ operationalize it,Â andÂ theÂ data shows the impact of their ability to do so.
AÂ separateÂ Microsoft-ledÂ study6Â of 1,800 workers globally foundÂ whenÂ managers actively modeled AI use, employees reported aÂ 17-pointÂ lift inÂ reportedÂ AI value7, aÂ 22-pointÂ lift in critical thinking about their AI use, and aÂ 30-pointÂ lift in trust in agentic AI. When managers created psychological safety around experimentation, employees reported up toÂ 20 pointsÂ higher AI readiness andÂ valueâand wereÂ 1.4xÂ more likely to be high-frequency users of agentic AI.
The Transformation Paradox is, at its core, a systems problem. And systemsÂ donâtÂ fix themselvesâtheyÂ have toÂ be redesigned.
Frontier ProfessionalsÂ in our survey consistently work in this kind of environment. Compared to nonâFrontier Professionals, they are significantly more likely to say their managerÂ openly uses AIÂ (85% vs. 64%), sets quality standards for AI work (83% vs. 57%),Â creates space for experimentation (84% vs. 61%), and encourages more ambitious work redesign (87% vs. 61%). They are also 2X more likely to say they are rewarded for the reinvention of work with AIÂ regardless of outcome (26%Â vs.Â 11%).
Individual potentialÂ canÂ compound when leadership setsÂ direction,Â culture supports experimentation and learning, and management practices reinforce new ways of working.
Dr. Karim Lakhani
Professor of Business Administration
Harvard Business School
Organizations
The firms pulling ahead areÂ focused on AI absorption ratherÂ than justÂ AI adoption,Â redesigning how work gets done and turning output into insight. When that insightÂ gets captured, shared, and built into how the organization operates, it creates a self-reinforcing Learning System.
Many leadersÂ focus on hiring the right people and assume results will follow.Â But our dataÂ showsÂ thatÂ itâsÂ something else: the conditionsÂ leaders create for that talent to thrive.
WeÂ analyzed responses fromÂ our global survey and tested a broad set of organizational, individual, and demographic factors against self-reported AI impact8âwhether employees say AIÂ helps them produce higher quality work, collaborate more effectively, expand the type of work they do,Â and more.
The resultsÂ show thatÂ organizational factors9Â likeÂ culture, manager support, and talent practicesÂ account forÂ more thanÂ 2xÂ theÂ reportedÂ AI impact of individual factors like mindset and behavior (67% vs. 32%).
AI Value
Organizational factorsâculture, manager support, talent practicesâaccount for more than 2x of AIâs real impact (67%) as individual mindset and behavior (32%).
Microsoft WTI 2026 Global Survey | 10 markets (US, BR, AU, IN, JP, FR, DE, IT, NL, UK), fielded by Edelman Data x Intelligence, February 18âApril 20, 2026 | Analyzed n = 20,000 sample; 19,854 analysis sample after listwise removal on 29 predictors | Bars show random forest permutation importance, normalized so the top factor equals 100 percent. Ranking holds across three model familiesâtest RÂ² of 0.680 (elastic net), 0.689 (random forest), and 0.690 (XGBoost) | 29 factors: 10 organizational, 9 individual, 10 demographic | Outcome is a 10-item Q27 composite measuring self-reported AI outcomes. Predictors are self-reported perceptions of the respondentâs work, workplace, and AI use. Values show a statistical association, not a causal effect.
The findings underscore the importance of an AI-ready environment: a culture thatÂ treatsÂ AI as a strategic advantage andÂ encourages experimentation, managers who model and incentivize AI use, and talent practices that build skills and create space to apply them.
TheÂ real questionÂ isnâtÂ whether people have the right skills. ItâsÂ whether the organization is built to unlock them.
15x
The number ofÂ activeÂ agents in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem has grown 15x year over year, rising to 18x in large enterprises.10
Asâ¯agents take on more, they also generate valuableÂ signals: what worked, what failed, where outcomes drifted. In many organizations surveyed, those signals stay local or spread slowly. Frontier Firms treat them differently.â¯They capture these signals and encode them into shared routines, improving futureÂ workâ¯while preserving accountability and control.
State of agents
Agents are now used in every industry, but the pattern of adoption varies widely.
Microsoft 365 Copilot agent telemetry | March 2025 through March 2026 | All metrics expressed as shares and ratios. No absolute counts.
For example,Â Frontier Professionals are more likely than nonâFrontier Professionals to say their teams brainstorm and refine business processes together to identify AI opportunities (63% vs. 32%),Â share AI tips, new agents, learnings, and mistakesÂ (61% vs.Â 36%), and discuss quality standards for AI-assisted workÂ (54% vs.Â 29%).
They are alsoÂ more likely to report that agent workflows, human handoffs, and quality standards are documented and repeatable at theÂ teamÂ (26% vs. 19%), function (29% vs. 17%), and organization levelÂ (25% vs.Â 14%).
ItÂ starts with three questions that every Frontier Firm will need to answer:Â Who reviews agent performance?Â Who has the authority to update the workflows that agents run? How does a local win get captured and scaled across the organization?Â Organizations that can answer these questions are building Owned Intelligenceâinstitutional know-how that compounds over time, isÂ unique to the firm,Â and is hard to replicate.
Every Frontier Firm needs to build OwnedÂ IntelligenceâinstitutionalÂ know-howÂ that compounds over time, isÂ unique to the firm,Â and is hard to replicate.
Building that infrastructure also requires coordinated reinvention across four roles: employees, who rearchitect their work around intent and review; leaders, who redesign processes around outcomes and agent autonomy; IT, who builds the infrastructure for agent operations at scale; and security, who ensures that trust is woven into the system itself.
For IT leaders, this means treating agents as managed entities with identities, permissions, policy enforcement, and lifecycle management. IT becomes the control plane for agent operations, extending the same rigor already applied to people and applications so that scale does not come at the cost of visibility.
For security leaders, this means accounting for the new risk that agents introduce: data exfiltration, unintended system actions, and unauthorized access. Securing agents requires embedding monitoring, policy enforcement, and auditability directly into the platform, so that trust operates as a structural property of the system.
When these four roles work in concert, the organization becomes a Learning System: one in which work continuously produces insight, and insight continuously reshapes how work gets done.
Meghana Dhar
Founder
Tea in Tech
Take action
The firms that build a new operating model todayÂ wonâtÂ just move faster in the short term.Â TheyâllÂ build something more durable, setting themselves up to create value in ways that we canât yet conceive of: an organization that learns faster than its competitors, compounds its own intelligence, and gets harder to catch with every cycle.
This shiftÂ wonâtÂ happen easily. Some jobs will change. Some will go away. And many that donât exist yet will emerge. According to LinkedInâsÂ 2026Â Labor Market Report, in the past two years, employers have created at least 1.3 million AI-related job opportunities, which include data annotators, AI engineers, and forward-deployed engineers. These roles didnât exist five years ago, but they have quickly become essential to digital economies. ThisÂ kind of dynamismÂ isnâtÂ new to work, but the pace and scale of it areâand the uncertainty people feel is real.
WhatâsÂ alsoÂ real:Â TheÂ potentialÂ for employees to make impact has never been higher. Leaders are starting to redesign the systems around them.Â The organizations capturing what their work is teaching themÂ areÂ learning faster than the onesÂ thatÂ arenât.Â None of that happens by accident.
The opportunity inÂ frontÂ of every leader and organization is to take control: to build a place where agents amplify what people can do,Â where human judgment stays at the center of the work that matters, and where we all have the agency to decide what comes next. This is what AI can mean for all of usâif we choose to do the work toÂ get there.

Frontier Professionals:Â ToÂ identifyÂ Frontier Professionals, we used a definition grounded in how peopleÂ self-report how theyÂ areÂ workingÂ withÂ AI.Â Respondents were classified as Frontier Professionals only if theyÂ reportedÂ a combination of three distinctÂ sets ofÂ behaviors:Â Advanced use of AI agents to complete complex or multi-step work;Â routine redesign of workflows to take advantage of what AI can do well;Â participation in structured, repeatable AI-enabled practices that can scale beyond individual use.Â TheyÂ representÂ 3,233 of the 20,000 AI users surveyed.Â 44% are business decision makers,Â andÂ 56% areÂ employees.Â 50% are millennials,Â 23% GenÂ X, 22% Gen Z,Â andÂ 4% Boomers.Â Frontier Professionals are more likely to work in tech (35%) or financial services (12%), with roles in IT (36%) or finance and accounting (11%). title: Enterprise AI Agents: Beyond Productivity | IBM
article_text:
AI agents, capable of orchestrating complex workflows to support human workers, help enterprises meet escalating business demands. They combine large language models (LLMs), machine learning, reasoning capabilities and external tool integration to handle complex and nuanced work. They parse context and adapt to changing circumstances, allowing them to help users streamline processes and improve decision-making across an organization.
Traditional automation long handled repetitive, rule-based tasks. And in recent years, generative AI (gen AI) transformed the business ecosystem, delivering AI assistants and other technologies designed to reduce workload and deliver delightful user experiences. AI agents represent a new paradigm—intelligent systems that choose strategies, learn from outcomes and act autonomously with minimal human supervision to achieve specific goals.
Agentic AI stands to fundamentally redefine how businesses operate. Traditionally, enterprise software helped workers organize data or complete tasks. But today, artificial intelligence has the potential to operate autonomously alongside human employees, ushering in a new era of human-machine partnerships.
Get curated insights on the most important—and intriguing—AI news. Subscribe to our twice-weekly Think Newsletter.
This evolution matters because enterprises face increasingly complex challenges: Handling customer inquiries requires understanding intent and emotion—as well as meeting consumer expectations of continuous support. Supply chain decisions demand real-time analysis of variables too complex for a single human to understand. Strategic planning involves synthesizing information from a vast number of disparate sources.
Increasingly, enterprises use AI in HR, procurement, sales, finance and IT departments to increase efficiency and reduce routine manual work. In recent years, IBM deployed agentic AI internally across a wide variety of workflows and functions to 270,000 employees. The initiative resulted in an estimated USD 4.5 billion productivity impact.
The shift toward agentic AI is industry-wide: Gartner predicts 60% of IT operations will incorporate AI agents by 2028. Forrester forecasts the world’s top five human resources management platforms will offer digital employee management capabilities in the coming year.
Beyond simple productivity gains, agentic AI transforms enterprise operating models. When agentic AI is embedded across departments and functions, its ability to make accurate, real-time decisions increases dramatically. With manual work performed by digital workers, employees necessarily shift focus to more value-driven work.
Today, enterprise data originates from a wide range of sources, spanning financial records, digital collaboration software and customer relationship management (CRM) platforms. Unifying this data reduces redundancies across platforms and allows for more accurate business-level forecasting.
In contrast to earlier AI capabilities, modern intelligent agents are capable of autonomy and draw on external tools or APIs to orchestrate workflows from end to end. Multi-agent systems collaborate across systems to complete a goal.
Often confused with AI assistants, AI agents draw on similar technologies but are proactive, rather than reactive, in nature. Where an AI assistant can complete a task in response to a user command or prompt, AI agents plan and execute multi-step processes based on an initial prompt. Some key features of enterprise AI agents include:
Rather than implementing a fixed sequence of steps, AI agents work toward objectives. For example, telling an agent to resolve a billing discrepancy would result in the agent determining the necessary steps—checking account history, identifying errors and communicating with users. This approach happens without requiring explicit instruction for each action.
Contextual understanding allows agents to interpret information within broader business contexts. This level of comprehension allows agents to work with more ambiguous instructions and incomplete information, much as human employees do.
Depending on the number of tools and APIs AI agents are granted permissions for, they’re able to not just suggest solutions but execute them. This capability might mean querying a database, generating a report, sending a message or triggering a workflow. This ability makes them genuine productivity multipliers rather than sophisticated chatbots.
Learning and adaptation allow agents to improve over time. They observe which approaches succeed, refining their strategies in the process.
Multi-step reasoning allows agents to break complex tasks into manageable components. This approach allows them to develop strategies and execute multi-phase plans. When asked to analyze market opportunities, for instance, an agent might identify relevant data sources, gather information, analyze findings and present recommendations.
Dramatic productivity gains emerge as agents handle work that previously required substantial time and reduced the amount of energy that human workers were able to devote to high-value tasks. Manual processes that once took weeks compress into days or hours. And employees who once spent days on data complication and analysis redirect that time toward strategic thinking and relationship building.
Implementing enterprise-wide AI systems removes data silos and reduces reliance on fragmented workflows. This approach reduces errors and provides a more holistic view of an organization’s operations, as well as saving time otherwise spent on replicating processes.
Decision quality improves with agents’ ability to process vast information volumes and identify patterns a human might miss. For example, an AI agent-assessing supplier performance simultaneously considers market trends, quality metrics and contractual terms—synthesizing insights that might take a team of analysis days or weeks to compile manually.
Agents’ always-on capacity provides capabilities impossible with human-only teams. Agents respond to customer or employee inquiries at any time of day, across time zone and apply policies uniformly. This means seamless global operations without expensive staffing redundancies.
Scalability without proportional cost increase fundamentally changes a business’ bottom line. AI agents handle volume spikes without extra costs.
Reduced human error in routine operations improves quality and reduces costly mistakes. Agents don’t mis-transcribe numbers or forget steps. In compliance-sensitive industries, this reliability provides substantial risk mitigation.
Among the earliest adopters of agentic AI, the customer service industry has come to embrace the technology: According to the IBM Institute for Business Value, by 2027 executives forecast a shift fully toward autonomous automation, with 71% aiming for touchless customer support inquiries. Modern customer service agents handle inquiries across channels such as email, chat and voice, understanding context and sentiment.
These agents resolve common issues autonomously, from resetting passwords to order tracking and basic troubleshooting. Beyond such reactive support, AI agents proactively identify customers experiencing difficulties and, if empowered, reach out with assistance. They can also analyze support conversations to identify product issues and improvement opportunities, creating a continuous feedback loop between customers and product teams.
IBM integrates AI into both its client and support experiences. An AI-driven tool resolved 70% of inquiries and time to resolution improved by 26%.
AI agents orchestrate complex business processes that span multiple systems and require adaptive decision-making. Unlike traditional workflow automation that follows rigid logic, AI agents optimize processes in real-time.
In procurement, agents can manage entire purchase-to-pay cycles—identifying needs, researching suppliers, generating purchase orders and processing invoices. When the B2B firm Dun & Bradstreet implemented an AI tool to streamline risk evaluation and vendor selection, for instance, it found the time spent on procurement tasks reduced up to 20%.
And for project management, AI agents coordinate team activities and monitor progress. They schedule meetings, prepare agendas and generate process reports highlighting risks and opportunities.
AI agents democratize sophisticated analytics, making granular data-driven insights accessible to employees without specialized trainings. They can translate natural language questions into more complex queries and analyze the results, presenting findings in intuitive formats.
These agents, given the right tools, also proactively highlight anomalies. They might monitor key performance indicators, alerting stakeholders to concerning trends before they become crisis.
AI agents transform IT operations from reactive troubleshooting to predictive and proactive systems. They monitor infrastructure health, detect anomalies, diagnose issues and often resolve problems.
For cybersecurity, AI agents provide continuous threat detection and response. They analyze network traffic and identify suspicious activities, implementing containment measures when necessary.
Agents also enhance software development operations by automating testing and monitoring application performance—even suggesting code optimizations. In collaboration with human DevOps teams, they handle routine tasks while flagging issues requiring human expertise.
In manufacturing environments, AI agents optimize production planning, quality control and maintenance operations. They proactively analyze demand forecasts and inventory levels along with material availability to keep production lines efficient. Predictive maintenance agents analyze equipment performance data to forecast failures before they occur, scheduling maintenance during optimal windows to minimize production disruption. This shift from reactive to predictive maintenance dramatically reduces unplanned downtime and extends equipment lifespans.
Supply chain agents can also manage the intricacies of manufacturing, continuously adjusting procurement logistics based on production needs, transportation availability and other variables. These implementations can have impressive results:
In recent years, IBM Consulting® applied AI across its global supply chain, an initiative spanning over 2,000 suppliers and operating in more than 170 countries. These agents identified risk and validated supplier commitments, among other tasks, resulting in over USD 361 in supplier savings over three years.
AI agents are reshaping talent management across the HR lifecycle, personalizing the employee experience and streamlining multiple administrative processes. Today, IBM’s AskHR tool automates more than 80 HR tasks and handles over 2.1 million employee conversations annually. And recently, SAP introduced agentic AI into its HCM platform, helping employees build career plans and manage payroll, among other functions.
In the recruitment process, agents source candidates and screen applications—reducing time-to-hire while improving candidate quality. For new hires, onboarding technology guides employees through paperwork and files necessary paperwork, personalizing and simplifying the process. And for ongoing employee support agentic HR can be a critical support for human employees, handling time-off requests and policy questions as well as necessary compliance paperwork.
Given AI agents’ ability to process large amounts of numerical data, financial services and operations stand to benefit enormously from the technology. Some agents might match invoices to purchase orders or receipts, while others flag discrepancies in ledgers. In expense management, agents process reimbursements or proactively detect potential fraud.
Financial planning and analysis AI solutions gather data from across an organization to generate forecasts or model various scenarios. For instance, IBM used AI to pinpoint the cost of its IT operations and drive USD 600 million in savings since 2022.
This helps translate complex financial information into accessible insights, supporting better decision-making throughout the organization. And in compliance, agents continuously monitor transactions against regulatory requirements, alerting teams to potential violations before they escalate.
Implementing AI agents successfully requires thoughtful planning and phased execution. Organizations that treat deployment as a technical project often struggle; those organizations that approach it as a business transformation initiative, enabled by technology, have a better chance to thrive.
Rather than pursuing AI or its own sake, identify specific challenges where agents deliver tangible, real-world value. Prioritize high-volume, time-consuming tasks and identify what success looks like—whether that’s increased employee satisfaction, faster resolution rates or customer adoption.
AI agent systems, as with other AI models, are only as effective as the data they consume. Evaluate whether the necessary, high-quality data exists and ensure it’s accessible. Prioritize data integrity: resolve quality issues and invest time in cleansing and standardizing datasets.
AI-powered solutions range from pre-built, enterprise-grade applications to customizable platforms and no-code tools. Some organizations build AI agents from scratch. Consider your technical capacity, customization needs and time-to-value requirements and choose a trusted partner.
The most successful implementations don’t replace humans with agents but create effective partnerships. Define clear handoff protocols and establish feedback mechanisms so agents learn from human interventions.
Establish guidelines for appropriate agent use. Implement monitoring and ensure that agents behave as intended. Create clear accountability frameworks defining responsibility when agents act autonomously. Prioritize observability and security for agentic AI over the long-term, and implement strict data retention and access control policies.
Communicate clearly, early and often about how agents will improve the employee experience—as well as which workflows will change. Empower employees with robust training programs so they understand how AI-driven tools work, as well as develop new skills as their roles evolve.
Establish processes for monitoring agent effectiveness from day one, gathering feedback and continuously refining performance. Measure agent performance against the KPIs established early in the planning process—and share results throughout the organization.
According to the IBM Institute for Business Value, among organizations that have adopted generative AI, only one-third report implementing the technology into functional processes. To embrace the promise of agentic AI, organizations must integrate the technology into everyday workforce tools and think critically about how human‑machine partnerships can transform operating models.
Agentic AI represents more than an incremental improvement in enterprise productivity—it signals a large-scale transformation in how work gets done. Realizing this potential requires more than purchasing technology. It demands to reimagine processes and to redefine roles, as well as cultivating an organizational culture of innovation. When businesses unify data and deeply integrate agentic AI systems at the enterprise level, they stand to build more resilient and adaptive organizations.
